idiom_name: per-object lock + one condition variable per wait reason, with predicate loops
implementation_notes: Define the object's state, one lock per object and one condition variable per distinct reason a method may have to wait. Every public method takes the lock, runs only the state access that needs it, and releases on every exit path (scoped locking); a method that cannot proceed waits on its condition inside a loop that re-tests the predicate, which releases the lock while suspended and re-acquires it before returning. Separate the interface methods that lock and signal from the implementation methods that assume the lock is held, so intra-object calls never re-enter the lock (the Thread-Safe Interface idiom). Match the mechanism to the runtime: a mutex plus condition variables for blocking code, an async lock or queue for coroutine and callback code, and a mailbox or a single-threaded executor when ownership can be confined instead of shared.
code_sketch:
put(item):                          # synchronized method
    lock()
    try:
        while is_full():            # predicate loop: re-test after every wakeup
            not_full.wait()         # releases lock, re-acquires it on return
        enqueue(item)               # implementation method, assumes the lock
        not_empty.notify()          # signal the waiters the state change helps
    finally:
        unlock()
pitfalls: Locking in client code instead of in the object reintroduces the coupling the pattern removes, and a single forgotten lock silently breaks the invariant.
Waiting outside a predicate loop, or notifying while the state change is not yet visible under the lock, produces lost and spurious wakeups that surface only under load.
Calling foreign code, a listener or another monitor's blocking method while holding the lock causes nested monitor lockout and inflates lock hold times.

Wrong move: call a blocking monitor method from an event-loop callback -> the event-loop thread stalls and unrelated tasks stop making progress -> instead use an async mutex or queue, or confine the state to the event loop.

Wrong move: treat a timeout or cancellation wakeup as proof that the predicate is true -> the method proceeds with unavailable state or leaks capacity -> instead re-check the predicate after every wait and return an explicit timeout or cancellation result.

Wrong move: use one notify or signal for waiters guarding different predicates -> an unrelated waiter wakes, consumes the signal and leaves the real waiter blocked -> instead use separate conditions, or broadcast and re-test each predicate under the lock.
